blocks.text: The fossil record shows that prokaryotes, archaea and bacteria, were abundant 3.5 billion years ago. They evolved and remained all alone on Earth for the next 2 billion years. Today prokaryotes are found wherever there is life. Bacteria live in water, air, soil, food and in the bodies of animals and plants. They outnumber all eukaryotes, and they can survive in extreme habitats.
Diversity in bacteria and their ecology
Margulis and Schwartz proposed a useful classification system for all prokaryotes, dividing them into 16 phyla. The important groups of domain Bacteria are described below.
1. Omnibacteria

Rigid, rod-shaped, heterotrophic, Gram-negative bacteria. Many important pathogens belong here. Most have flagella, they do not produce spores, and they are usually aerobic. Escherichia coli is an example; the group also includes vibrios.
2. Cyanobacteria

Photosynthetic bacteria that played the most important role in the history of the Earth by increasing free oxygen in the atmosphere. They contain chlorophyll a and accessory pigments such as carotenoids and blue and red phycobilins. Many cyanobacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen in special cells called heterocysts. They are common in soil as mats; cyanobacteria-containing lichens grow on rock surfaces; and the mats on sediments in the sea are dominated by cyanobacteria.

blocks.title: Cyanobacteria in the news
blocks.text: Perhaps most interesting of all is the recent discovery that the bulk of our modern petroleum deposits were formed by masses of decayed cyanobacteria. Colourful blooms may occur in polluted water as a result of the rampant growth of cyanobacteria; the colours of such blooms come from their photosynthetic pigments.
3. Mycoplasmas and spiroplasmas

These groups differ from all other bacteria in lacking cell walls. Because they have no wall, they are resistant to penicillin and other antibiotics that work by inhibiting cell-wall growth. Some mycoplasmas cause diseases in mammals, for example certain types of pneumonia in humans. Spiroplasmas cause significant plant diseases, such as the lethal yellowing disease of coconuts.
4. Spirochaetes
Long spirilla with Gram-negative cell walls. They may have from 2 to more than 100 flagella. Treponema are important spirochaetes: they cause syphilis, a fatal sexually transmitted disease.
5. Pseudomonads

Straight or curved Gram-negative rods with one or many flagella at one end. They are found in soil and water and can easily break down organic compounds. Some are autotrophic, but many are plant pathogens, and some play a role in denitrification. Pseudomonas aeruginosa occurs in soil, water and raw vegetables; although usually harmless, it can cause serious infections in weak people.
6. Actinomycetes

Bacteria with filamentous growth forms. They produce spores that resist unfavourable conditions. Some are nitrogen fixers found in the root nodules of many flowering plants. Some are responsible for dental plaque, in which the enamel of teeth is destroyed. Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy and Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculosis. Many antibiotics, such as tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin and neomycin, were originally derived from actinomycetes.

blocks.title: A source of antibiotics
blocks.text: About 150 new antibiotics from actinomycetes are being discovered each year.
7. Nitrogen-fixing aerobic bacteria
An economically important group of Gram-negative bacteria, most of them flagellated. Azotobacter is a member: it lives in soil and water and converts atmospheric nitrogen into nitrates.
8. Chemosynthetic bacteria

These bacteria derive energy from the oxidation of inorganic compounds of nitrogen, sulphur and iron, and use that energy to synthesise their food. Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter belong here: they oxidise nitrogen compounds (NH3) to gain energy, and the NH3 is in turn converted to nitrite and nitrate. In this way they play a vital role in the nitrogen cycle.
